lesson.title: Rearranging Real Formulas: From Science Class to Solving for Any Quantity
lesson.summary: Apply the skill of solving for a variable to real formulas from geometry, science, and finance, rearranging each one to solve for a different quantity as the situation demands.
lesson.body:
Formulas are written to compute one particular quantity, but the situation in front of you often gives you every value except a different one. The formula for simple interest, I = Prt, is set up to compute interest, but a problem might give the interest earned, the principal, and the rate, and ask for the time. Rather than memorizing a separate formula for every possible rearrangement, formula manipulation lets you start from one trusted formula and solve for whatever quantity you actually need, using the same equality-based moves practiced with literal equations.

The approach is to treat the formula exactly like a literal equation: identify the variable you want to isolate, look at every operation currently attached to it, and undo those operations in reverse order using inverse operations on both sides. It often helps to substitute any known numeric values into the formula first, before isolating the unknown, since working with a mix of known numbers and one unknown letter is usually simpler than manipulating an equation with several letters still in place.

Suppose a formula from geometry gives the area of a triangle as A = (1/2)bh, and a problem states the area is 24 square centimeters with a base of 6 centimeters, asking for the height. Substitute the known values first: 24 = (1/2)(6)h, which simplifies to 24 = 3h. Divide both sides by 3: h = 8. Check by substituting all three values back into the original formula: A = (1/2)(6)(8) = (1/2)(48) = 24, which matches the given area exactly, confirming the height is 8 centimeters.

The same formula can also be rearranged in general, before any numbers are known, by solving A = (1/2)bh for h directly: multiply both sides by 2 to get 2A = bh, then divide both sides by b to get h = 2A/b. Using the numbers from the example, h = 2(24)/6 = 48/6 = 8, the same answer found by substituting first, showing that solving for a variable in general and substituting numbers early are two equally valid paths that must agree.

The same rearranging shows up in the Fahrenheit-Celsius conversion formula, F = (9/5)C + 32, when a temperature is given in Fahrenheit and Celsius is needed instead. Subtract 32 from both sides: F - 32 = (9/5)C. Multiply both sides by 5/9 to isolate C: C = (5/9)(F - 32). Checking with F = 68 gives C = (5/9)(68 - 32) = (5/9)(36) = 20, and working forward from C = 20 confirms it: F = (9/5)(20) + 32 = 36 + 32 = 68, the temperature we started with.

Formula manipulation is where literal equations and solving for a variable become genuinely useful tools rather than abstract exercises, since almost every formula in science, finance, and geometry will eventually need to be solved for a variable other than the one it was written to compute. The habit to keep is the same one built throughout this unit: identify what operations sit on the target variable, and undo them one at a time using the properties of equality, whether the rest of the equation is full of numbers, other letters, or both.
